sentences.text: Cymbospondylus is an extinct genus of large ichthyosaurs.
This marine reptile possessed flippers for limbs and a fin on its tail.
The animal had an elongated, conical snout where the premaxillae and nasal bones were the largest skull elements.
It had two pairs of flippers and an eel-like tail, lacking a dorsal fin, with a length of approximately 6 to 10 meters.
While the color of Cymbospondylus is unknown, some early ichthyosaurs likely had uniformly dark skin, evidenced by preserved eumelanin pigments.
The largest known species, C. youngorum, was estimated to be over 17 meters long, making it one of the largest animals of its time.
C. youngorum is estimated to reach 17.65 meters in length and weigh 44.7 metric tons, making it one of the largest ichthyosaurs known.
Researchers describe C. youngorum as "the first aquatic giant" due to its early Middle Triassic age and massive size.
The largest known species, C. youngorum, had a skull measuring up to about 2 meters long.
The holotype of C. duelferi contains three strings of small vertebrae interpreted as the remains of three fetuses.
Fossil evidence suggests Cymbospondylus gave live birth to at least three offspring.
The Cymbospondylus appeared in the 2003 BBC docufiction Sea Monsters.
The genus Cymbospondylus was named and described by Joseph Leidy in 1868.
The first fossils of Cymbospondylus were discovered in the 19th century in Nevada, United States.
Joseph Leidy described Cymbospondylus in 1868 based on fossil vertebrae from Nevada, United States, which were transmitted to him by geologist Josiah Dwight Whitney.
Fossils have been found in Nevada, USA, and Switzerland.
Direct fossil evidence shows that C. buchseri ate soft-bodied coleoid cephalopods, as its stomach contents contained only their hooks.
Researchers suggest C. buchseri had a robust rostrum that supported a forceful feeding strategy with high bite force.
C. youngorum is inferred to have been a generalist predator of squid and fish, based on its blunt conical teeth and elongated rostrum.
Cymbospondylus lived alongside other abundant ichthyosaurs like Omphalosaurus, Phalarodon, and the large Thalattoarchon in the Fossil Hill Member.
The fossil assemblage indicates that the ancient surface waters where Cymbospondylus lived were well aerated.
Near-surface waters were well oxygenated and inhabited by plankton and free-swimming organisms.
Poor water circulation resulted in anoxic, oxygen-deprived water at the bottom of the lagoon.
Thalattoarchon was likely the only contemporary apex predator, probably attacking smaller marine reptiles or juveniles.
Stomach contents of Mixosaurus cornalianus show remains of small coleoids and fish, suggesting it hunted smaller prey than larger relatives.
It is agreed that Cymbospondylus is a basal member of the Ichthyosauria clade.
Recent studies classify Cymbospondylus as the type genus of the family Cymbospondylidae, rather than Shastasauridae.
The classification of Guizhouichthyosaurus tangae as a synonym of Shastasaurus was contested in 2010, with Michael W. Maisch provisionally reclassifying it as a distinct genus.
Researchers could not determine a definite placement for C. buchseri and stated further study is needed to confirm if it belongs to the genus.
Cymbospondylus lived during the Olenekian to Anisian stages of the Triassic period.
Three specimens from Idaho and Svalbard dated to the Olenekian stage of the Lower Triassic represent the oldest known members of the genus Cymbospondylus.
C. youngorum lived at the beginning of the Middle Triassic.
Cymbospondylus lived in marine ecosystems alongside bivalves, ammonites, Saurichthys, coelacanths, hybodonts, sauropterygians, and other ichthyosaurs.
In 2003, Christopher McGowan and Ryosuke Motani questioned the validity of C. piscosus, asserting its fossils lack distinctive characteristics.
